title: Young Mind Education — Hellenic Seed Curriculum

audience.notes: Designed for children who can listen to rich stories, narrate back, ask why/how questions, and begin proof-like thinking.

designIntent.oneSentence: A small, local-first corpus that lets Lectern suggest guided lessons by subject without becoming a bloated LMS or generic book list.
distillationRules: Prefer one high-yield anchor per intellectual habit: story, moral judgment, history, proof, observation, language, and beauty.
Prefer public-domain or locally-authored materials that can live inside the repo or a sibling local source library.
Prefer texts that can be chunked into short teachable units: fable, episode, life, map scene, proposition, nature observation, picture-study plate.
Do not treat commercial curricula as source texts. Store them only as optional owned-required metadata.
Start narrow: add expansion texts only when a learner has demonstrated narration, attention, and recall on the seed anchors.

statuses.public-domain-download: May be imported into the local source tree after jurisdiction/license check and source attribution.
statuses.public-domain-scan: Use a local OCR or manually cleaned edition from a public-domain scan; keep scan attribution in sidecar metadata.
statuses.local-original: Authored inside this repo or family library; safe to distribute with the app if the author permits.
statuses.curated-public-domain-assets: Images/music metadata selected from public-domain museum/library collections; store attribution per asset.
statuses.metadata-only: A target for future sourcing; do not assume text is locally present.
statuses.owned-required: Useful pedagogically, but not imported or redistributed; available only if the family owns a copy.

lessonOperations.label: Narrate
lessonOperations.description: The child tells the episode back in order, with names, places, and one striking phrase.

lessonOperations.label: Ask why
lessonOperations.description: The tutor asks one cause, motive, or justice question instead of a recall quiz.

lessonOperations.label: Map or timeline
lessonOperations.description: The child anchors an episode to a place, route, date range, ruler, or before/after sequence.

lessonOperations.label: Copy or memorize
lessonOperations.description: The child copies a sentence, term, name, root, definition, or beautiful phrase.

lessonOperations.label: Draw or demonstrate
lessonOperations.description: The child draws the proof, animal, plant, tool, artwork, route, or scene and explains it.

lessonOperations.label: Compare
lessonOperations.description: The child compares two heroes, choices, proofs, observations, or works of art.

seedBundle.title: The Eight-Anchor Hellenic Seed
seedBundle.description: The minimal corpus I would start with before adding a broader classics shelf.
weeklyLoop: 1 short Aesop-style virtue discussion as warmup or review
completionEvidence: Child narrated at least 12 story/history episodes without heavy prompting.
Child placed at least 10 people/events/places on a map or timeline.
Child demonstrated at least 6 geometry ideas with a drawing or physical model.
Child made at least 8 nature or art observations in their own words.
Child copied or remembered at least 20 Greek/Latin names, roots, or phrases.

sourceTexts.title: Aesop's Fables: A New Translation
sourceTexts.author: Aesop; V. S. Vernon Jones, translator; G. K. Chesterton, commentator; Arthur Rackham, illustrator
sourceTexts.whyDistilled: The shortest high-yield unit in the corpus: one fable can produce narration, moral judgment, analogy, and a child's own example in ten minutes.

recommendedScope.selectionNotes: Choose animal and civic fables first; avoid using the whole book as a march-through assignment.

guidedPrompts: Tell the fable back in three beats: problem, choice, consequence.
Was the character foolish, wicked, unlucky, or simply unprepared?
Invent a modern version of the same fable.

sourceTexts.title: The Adventures of Odysseus and The Tales of Troy
sourceTexts.author: Padraic Colum; Willy Pogány, illustrator
sourceTexts.whyDistilled: One book gives the Trojan frame, Odysseus, Telemachus, homecoming, gods, hospitality, courage, pride, cunning, and enough elevated diction to prepare later Homer without forcing a young child into adult translations.

recommendedScope.selectionNotes: Use as the main epic spine. Chunk by episode, not by page count.

guidedPrompts: What did the hero want, and what did the hero risk?
Was this victory won by strength, counsel, courage, patience, or deceit?
Place this episode on the Troy-to-Ithaca route or Trojan War timeline.

sourceTexts.title: Famous Men of Greece
sourceTexts.author: John H. Haaren and A. B. Poland
sourceTexts.whyDistilled: Biography is the most compact way to give a child Greek chronology: lawgivers, poets, generals, philosophers, and kings become timeline pegs rather than disconnected facts.

recommendedScope.selectionNotes: Start with Lycurgus/Solon, Miltiades/Themistocles, Pericles, Socrates, Alexander. Add others as review or enrichment.

guidedPrompts: What problem did this person try to solve?
Did this person serve a city, a family, an army, himself, or the truth?
Add this life to the Greek timeline with one sentence of memory.

local.upstream: Local scan/OCR or public-domain library scan of the 1904 edition; avoid modern revised editions unless rights are clear.

sourceTexts.title: The Boys' and Girls' Herodotus
sourceTexts.author: Herodotus; John S. White, editor
sourceTexts.whyDistilled: This is the first bridge from retold history into the historian's habit: asking what happened, who says so, where it happened, and whether a story is trustworthy.

recommendedScope.selectionNotes: Use Croesus, Cyrus, Egypt/customs, Marathon, Thermopylae, Salamis, and one wonder-tale.

guidedPrompts: What did Herodotus see, hear, or report second-hand?
Find the place on a map before discussing the story.
What question would you ask Herodotus if he were in the room?

local.upstream: Local scan/OCR or public-domain library scan of John S. White edition.

sourceTexts.title: Pre-Euclid Geometry Cards
sourceTexts.author: Local original, drawing on public-domain elementary geometry traditions
sourceTexts.whyDistilled: Before formal proof, a child needs to see, draw, fold, rotate, compare, and name geometric realities. A local card deck can be shorter and cleaner than any 19th-century textbook.

recommendedScope.selectionNotes: Cards should be physical-action first: draw, fold, cut, construct, explain.

guidedPrompts: Draw it two ways, then explain what stayed the same.
What definition would let another person recognize this figure?
Can you make a counterexample?

local.upstream: Authored locally; may cite Thomas Hill-style pre-Euclidean visual habits in notes, but do not require his text for the seed.

sourceTexts.title: Euclid Book I: Definitions, Common Notions, and Selected Propositions
sourceTexts.displayTitle: Euclid Book I — Visual Proof Pack
sourceTexts.author: Euclid; John Casey edition; Oliver Byrne visual reference
sourceTexts.whyDistilled: A small selection from Book I teaches that math is ordered speech and visible reasoning, not just answer-getting. Byrne-style diagrams make the beauty visible while Casey-style text keeps the proof tradition nearby.

recommendedScope.selectionNotes: Use definitions, postulates/common notions, propositions I.1, I.5, I.13, I.15, I.26, I.29, I.32, I.47 as a long arc.

guidedPrompts: What is given, what is required, and what is proven?
Redraw the figure without letters, then explain the proof in your own words.
Which earlier idea does this proof depend on?

local.upstream: Project Gutenberg eBook 21076 for Casey text; Byrne diagrams from public-domain scan where stored separately with attribution.

sourceTexts.title: Handbook of Nature Study — Selected Local Observations
sourceTexts.author: Anna Botsford Comstock; local selections and prompts
sourceTexts.whyDistilled: A small set of local nature prompts prevents science from becoming abstract too early. The child must look, name, draw, describe, and wonder before receiving explanations.

recommendedScope.selectionNotes: Do not import the whole 900-page handbook as the first experience. Build local seasonal prompts: bird, tree, flower, insect, sky, weather, water, stone.

guidedPrompts: Look silently for one minute before naming anything.
Draw what you actually see, then write three exact observations.
What changed since the last time you saw this?

local.upstream: Local excerpts from a verified public-domain scan of Handbook of Nature Study; prompts localized by family/teacher.

sourceTexts.title: Greek & Latin Starter Cards
sourceTexts.author: Local original
sourceTexts.whyDistilled: A child does not need a full grammar course to begin. The concentrated seed is alphabet comfort, beautiful names, roots that unlock English, and the idea that language has form.

recommendedScope.selectionNotes: 24 Greek letters, 12 Homer/history names, 20 Latin/Greek roots, 6 grammar-shape cards.

guidedPrompts: Copy the letter/name carefully and say it aloud.
Find an English word that carries this root.
Which names from today's story contain sounds you can now recognize?

local.upstream: Authored locally from standard alphabet/root knowledge and names encountered in seed texts.

sourceTexts.title: Greek Art & Architecture Picture Study Pack
sourceTexts.author: Local curator; public-domain museum/library assets where verified
sourceTexts.whyDistilled: A tiny image set makes beauty concrete: the child studies form, proportion, courage, grief, victory, and public memory without needing an art-history textbook.

recommendedScope.selectionNotes: Start with Parthenon, Caryatid, Discobolus, Winged Victory, Laocoön, Greek vase scene, Doric/Ionic/Corinthian columns, one map/plan of Athens.

guidedPrompts: Look for three minutes, then hide the image and describe it.
What line, shape, gesture, or proportion makes it beautiful or memorable?
Connect this work to a person, city, virtue, or geometry idea.

local.upstream: Verified public-domain/open-access museum and library assets, stored with per-asset attribution.

nearExpansionCandidates.title: Tanglewood Tales
nearExpansionCandidates.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
nearExpansionCandidates.addWhen: The learner needs a gentler myth bridge or wants more pre-Homer Greek mythology.
nearExpansionCandidates.whyNotSeed: Useful, but overlaps with Aesop plus Colum; keep as prelude/enrichment rather than a required core.

nearExpansionCandidates.title: The Story of the Greeks
nearExpansionCandidates.author: H. A. Guerber
nearExpansionCandidates.addWhen: The learner needs a smoother narrative history spine after or alongside selected Famous Men lives.
nearExpansionCandidates.whyNotSeed: Excellent, but duplicates some function of Famous Men. Add when more story-continuity is needed.

nearExpansionCandidates.title: The Golden Fleece and the Heroes Who Lived Before Achilles
nearExpansionCandidates.author: Padraic Colum
nearExpansionCandidates.addWhen: The learner loves Colum and needs the Argonaut/pre-Achilles myth cycle.
nearExpansionCandidates.whyNotSeed: Beautiful and coherent, but the first seed should not become an all-myth shelf.

nearExpansionCandidates.title: The Story of the Iliad
nearExpansionCandidates.author: Alfred J. Church
nearExpansionCandidates.addWhen: The learner finishes Colum and needs a more linear war narrative before selected adult Homer.
nearExpansionCandidates.whyNotSeed: Second-pass Iliad clarity, not the first epic spine.

nearExpansionCandidates.title: The Story of the Odyssey
nearExpansionCandidates.author: Alfred J. Church
nearExpansionCandidates.addWhen: The learner wants more episode clarity and map work after Colum.
nearExpansionCandidates.whyNotSeed: Second-pass Odyssey clarity, not required at launch.

nearExpansionCandidates.title: First Lessons in Geometry
nearExpansionCandidates.author: Thomas Hill
nearExpansionCandidates.addWhen: The local Pre-Euclid cards need a fuller public-domain textual ancestor or teacher reference.
nearExpansionCandidates.whyNotSeed: Harder to source cleanly than local cards plus public-domain Euclid; use as reference after the card deck exists.

local.upstream: Sourcing target; verify scan/license before import.

nearExpansionCandidates.title: Selected Greek Lives
nearExpansionCandidates.author: Plutarch; public-domain English translation or child adaptation
nearExpansionCandidates.addWhen: The learner can compare character, motive, civic choice, and consequence across multiple lives.
nearExpansionCandidates.whyNotSeed: Plutarch is central later, but Famous Men is a cleaner first biography spine for age 10.

doNotImportAsSeed.reason: Pedagogically useful, but modern copyright; keep as owned-required metadata only.
Strong structured course, but commercial curriculum; do not treat as local source text.
Useful Greek intro, but commercial; local starter cards cover the app-native seed need.
Too large for guided suggestions; use selected localized observations first.

avoid: suggesting a broad new book before the seed bundle has evidence of completion
turning every lesson into comprehension questions
using modern commercial resources as if they are bundled source texts
suggesting source text that has local.status metadata-only unless parent has enabled it
